title: Chapter 76 – What Heng Knew
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The chit arrives at the Pill Hall the morning after the trial, folded small, with the Library's gray seal pressed into the wax.

Disciple Lin Jian, Outer Sect 0417. By the leave of Elder Qin Hao and the Arbiter, you are asked to attend the Library Annex at the second bell after noon. The request is a request. It cannot be compelled.

Jian reads it twice in the herb store, between the bitterwort and the dried bark, and puts it in his sleeve.

He has been expecting it for eleven days. A man in a red silk chair said it aloud in front of the whole Court: I would like to see him. It was reported in every mouth the Outer Court owns, which is to say, in every courtyard, every kitchen and every washhouse. The Red Ridge man wants the Pill Hall boy. Ma Bao has it by nightfall. Hua Ning has it by dawn.

"You will not go," says Steward Gu, to the bark.

"It says it cannot be compelled."

"It says that. Such letters always do." The steward weighs a pinch and scowls. "A request from an Elder of the Library is the sort of request one accepts, if one wishes to go on being someone who is asked."

"Then I will go."

"Hm." Gu looks up. His eyes are small and bright and unhappy. "He is a dying man in a cold cell, Lin Jian. Dying men are very persuasive. They have nothing left to be careful of."

"Yes, Steward."

"Take a lamp," says Gu. "The Annex is dark."

* * *

Elder Bai is in the furnace room when Jian goes to ask leave, sitting beside the bronze with the jade dome closed over the red box and nothing in his mouth.

"Library," he says, when he has read the chit. "Qin Hao's Annex."

"Yes, Elder."

"You will go."

"I have said I will."

"Of course you have." The round face is unreadable. "I would not stop you. I have no standing to stop you. I am only a person who has kept a pill on a shelf for fifty-two years, and has a particular interest in whatever Heng thinks he knows." He turns the chit over. "Do you know what the Sect's first Elders called the disciple the pill was made for?"

"No, Elder."

"They did not call him anything. That is my point." Bai sets the chit down. "It is in the Pill Hall's oldest ledger. A line, six hundred years old, in the Founder's own ink. One pill, Level 2, peak, for the child. No name. No rank. I asked my master about it, when I was young. He told me not to ask again." He lifts his eyes. "I did not. For sixty years. And then you stood at that ring and told me about a knot."

Jian says nothing.

"Whatever the Red Ridge man tells you," says Bai, "he is selling it. He has been a merchant of other men's lives for thirty years. He will give you a true thing and a false thing, and make you pay for both." The pale eyes crease. "Count what you are given. And when you have counted it, tell me what is left. I will not ask for more."

"Yes, Elder."

"Go and sweep." A flick of the hand. "And take a lamp. The Annex is dark."

It is the second time I have been told that. Jian bows and goes.

* * *

The Library Annex stands behind the Library proper, a squat windowless building of black stone with a roof of green copper gone dull. There is a single door. Beside the door, on a bench, sits a lean figure in a gray cloak with his hands in his lap and his face turned to the sky.

"Inspector," says Jian.

"Disciple." Cheng Yun gets to his feet. His face is tired and a little thinner than it was at the ford, and there is a pale line on his collar where an Enforcement Hall badge once rested. "I am no longer an inspector. I report each morning to Elder Duan's clerk, and each noon to a different clerk, and each evening to a third. I am told it is a courtesy." His mouth twitches. "Elder Qin asked for me. He said you would prefer a face you knew."

"That was kind of him."

"It was calculated. He is a calculating man." Cheng Yun lowers his voice. "He is also, I think, a decent one. The two are less rare in the Library than elsewhere."

He opens the door.

Inside is a stair, narrow and steep, going down. The air is cold and smells of stone and dust and a faint sweet note of lamp oil. Jian lights Gu's lamp. The flame stands up straight and white, undisturbed by any draft. They descend in silence, past a landing, past another, until the stair opens on a long low corridor lit by a row of small blue lamps.

Cells line one side. Eight of them, each with a door of black iron with a round window the size of a plate. Frost glitters on the bars.

At the far end of the corridor, in a niche of its own, sits a ninth door.

It is not iron. It is wood, pale and plain, banded with silver. A silver pin, a hand's length, is driven through the lintel. And before the door, on a stool, with a book on his knee and a candle at his elbow, sits Qin Hao.

* * *

"You came," says the Elder.

"You asked, Elder."

"A great many people ask. Few come." The scholar closes his book. He is, up close, older than he looked in the Hall of Open Session: seventy, perhaps, with a long gray beard, eyes sunk in hollows and a hand that trembles very slightly when it is not occupied. He looks at Jian with an expression of mild, attentive interest. "Sit, if you like. There is a stool. I have been told to give you tea. I regret that I have not."

"I am not thirsty, Elder."

"You are twenty, and you have been told that I am dangerous. It is not an unreasonable precaution." Qin Hao smiles faintly. "I will tell you what I am. I am an old man who has read a great deal and understood very little. I am responsible for the man in that cell. I am obliged to be in the room while he talks. I do not mind. I have never found a conversation I could not learn from." He rises. "The door is a restricted-qi door. Nothing is cast through it. He cannot reach you, and you cannot reach him. You may speak. It is a conversation only."

"He asked for me, Elder. Why?"

"He did not say." The gray eyes rest on him. "I believe he intends to tell you."

He lays one hand flat against the silver-banded door and says a word in a very low voice, and the pin in the lintel gives a faint, high chime.

The door swings open.

Inside, there is a room.

It is not a cell as the others are. It is a chamber twelve paces long, with a rug, a low bed, a table and a reading lamp, and the walls are lined from floor to ceiling with scroll shelves. A brazier burns in one corner, small and red. In the center, in the black lacquer chair with the red silk cushions, sits Zhao Heng.

He has changed. The Hall of Open Session had shown a man composed and grim. This is a different man. His face is gaunter, almost transparent, and the black thread at the base of his throat has stopped at the jaw and become a faint gray scar. His hands lie in his lap, thin as bundled twigs. His eyes, large in the hollows of his face, are very bright.

"Lin Jian," he says, in his light dry voice. "You are smaller than I expected."

* * *

For a while neither speaks.

The brazier ticks. Qin Hao has taken a stool in the doorway and opened his book again, in the manner of a man who intends to be forgotten. Jian sets the lamp on the table. He does not sit. He stands three paces from the lacquer chair with his hands at his sides and looks, steadily, at the man who raised sixty armed men against his mother's house.

Heng looks back.

"You may hate me," he says at last. "I would not blame you. I would think less of you if you did not."

"I do not hate you."

"No?"

"It is a waste." Jian says it plainly. "You are a man who wanted a thing and used the people nearest to take it. I have met a few. The ones I hate are the ones who do not know they are doing it."

"And I do."

"You do."

"Yes." A faint dry smile. "That is the reason I wished to meet you. You see things as they are, and then you decline to be angry about them. It is a very rare gift. It is, I imagine, a kind of discipline." The smile fades. "You cracked my foundation, you know. You and your root, and your mother's Garden, and whatever you did with that machine of yours."

He knows about the machine. Jian keeps his face still. Not the Interface. The forge. The arm.

"It is a wound that will not close," Heng continues. "A year, they tell me. Perhaps two. I have spent the first few weeks of it reading. Elder Qin has been generous with the Annex. There are scrolls here that have not been opened since the Sect was founded." The bright eyes hold his. "I have found some things. I am going to sell them to you."

"I have no money."

"I do not want money."

"I have eighty points."

"I do not want points." A breath, shallow. "I want a thing, Lin Jian. I will ask for it later. Not now. I have no use for it now, and I do not know yet what shape it will take." He watches Jian's face. "You will find that irritating. I am sorry. It is the only currency a dying man has."

A favor.

Jian considers it with the whole of his attention. A favor, owed to a man with a Blood Shadow thread in his throat, to be named at a time of his choosing. It is an open ledger. It is the worst kind of debt, and the sort of thing his mother would refuse before the sentence was finished.

"I will not harm my family," he says.

"I did not ask you to."

"I will not kill for you. I will not take anything from the Garden or give anything away that belongs to my clan. I will not do a thing that breaks the Sect's rules in a way that would cost my brother his place."

"Those are three conditions."

"They are the three I can afford."

Heng laughs. It is a thin dry sound with something almost warm in it. "Elder Qin," he says, over his shoulder, "are you hearing this?"

"I am writing it down," says Qin Hao, without looking up.

"Good. It shall be witnessed." The pale eyes return to Jian. "Done. A favor, asked once, within a year, none of those three. If you refuse, I shall have no remedy. I am a man with a year to live. I would rather have your word than a bond." A pause. "Do you give it?"

A favor. A year.

He has one thing on his side, which is that he has been, all his short life, very careful about promises.

"I give it," he says.

It is a strange feeling, to have said it aloud.

Jian has made bargains before. He has made them with a one-armed forgemaster, a Patriarch, a Deputy of the Court, and each time he knew the weight of what he gave. This one has no weight at all. It floats, a thing without a shape, to be filled at a stranger's convenience. He looks at the dying man's face, the sharp bones, the bright patient eyes, and understands that Heng has chosen this price on purpose. He wants Jian to think about it every day.

A debt that is never called is a debt that is always paid.

He puts the thought away for later. It will keep. Behind him, in the doorway, Qin Hao turns a page of his book that he has not read, and the sound is very loud in the little room.

* * *

"Six hundred years ago," says Heng, "there was a child."

He has asked for tea, and Qin Hao has brought it, a thin steaming cup that rattles faintly in the saucer. He holds it in both hands, not drinking. The light of the brazier sits in the hollows of his face.

"I did not understand that he was a child until the third scroll. The Sect's histories call him the Disciple of the Fortieth Step. They do not give his name. They record that he came to the gate in the sixth year of the Founding, a boy of nine or ten, with his hair uncut and a bundle on his back, and that he asked to be admitted. The gate warden refused. The Founder came down the stair himself, and looked at the boy for a long time, and said: Let him in."

"Why?"

"Because he had five roots." Heng turns the cup. "Wood, fire, earth, metal and water. In equal measure. It is a thing that happens once in a thousand years, if the histories are to be trusted, and it is not an honor. A body with five roots casts everything slowly and nothing well. It is a cripple's gift." The smile is bitter. "The Founder did not take him for his gift. The Founder took him because of what he did."

Jian's mouth has gone dry.

"The boy walked into the Sect's garden," says Heng, "and the plants leaned toward him."

The Orchard.

"All of them. Every herb in the beds, every tree on the terrace. They bent. They did not wilt. They leaned, as a field of grass leans before a wind, and when he moved they moved. The Founder saw it from the stair. He said nothing for the length of a day. Then he summoned the first Elders, and told them the Sect would build something, and that the boy would be its heart."

"Its heart."

"The Garden." Heng's voice is almost gentle. "The thing the Court now holds in trust for ten years, on a hill called Green Pine, was not built by your clan's ancestor. It was a copy. A cutting from the first Garden, planted far from the Sect by a loyal man, in case of need. The first Garden was under this mountain."

Under the mountain.

"It was a vast work. I have read three accounts of its building and they do not agree. It was meant to do something, a single great thing, and it needed a child. A particular child. One whose Qi breathed." The cup rattles in the saucer. "And it needed a lock, so that no one but the right child could open it. The Founder built the lock into the Hundred Stairs."

"The fortieth step."

"Ah." Heng's bright eyes narrow. "You know."

"It is in the Precepts," says Jian, evenly. "The ninth. You cited it yourself."

"I did. I cited it for the Garden." A pause. "I did not cite what it says about the stair. It is the second clause. The trial of the Gate is a measure, not a purpose. The Founder's clerks have commented on it for six hundred years and decided it is a rhetorical flourish." He shakes his head slowly. "It is a statement of fact."

* * *

"What happened to him?" says Jian.

He is surprised by the sound of his own voice. It is quiet and rather flat.

Heng sets down the cup.

"The histories agree on one thing only. In the ninth year of the Founding, on a day in spring, the boy climbed the stair. He reached the fortieth step and he did not come down."

"He fell?"

"The Sect's record says fell. It is a very short record. It was written by a clerk, a long time later, who did not like to leave the page blank." The thin hands fold. "There is a second record in the Annex. It is in the Founder's own hand, on a strip of silk, and it was never copied. It is four lines long. It says:"

He closes his eyes. When he speaks again, his voice has changed. It is lower and slower and has the strange flat music of a thing recited from memory.

"He did not fall. He went in.

The door took him as a door takes a hand.

I have built it to be opened once more, by one like him.

Let the Sect be worthy, and let it wait."

The brazier ticks. In the doorway, Qin Hao has stopped reading. His lined face is turned toward the chair and he is utterly still.

"Six hundred years," says Heng, opening his eyes. "A child with five roots, a stair that is not a stair, and a Founder who built a door and waited for the right hand." His gaze fixes on Jian. "I have waited eleven days to say this to someone, and there is no one else it would be true for."

"I am not that child."

"You are the second."

"I am Lin Jian. I am the third son of a village clan."

"You are a boy with five roots," says Heng, "whose Qi breathes, who walked into a garden and made it bloom in winter, who cracked the foundation of a Late Foundation cultivator at the age of nine with a thing I have yet to understand. You stand on the fortieth landing for the length of one breath, and the array reads forty-two." The dry voice is as gentle as a hand on the shoulder. "I have friends in the Annex, Lin Jian. The keepers write things down."

Keeper Fu's other book.

It lies cold in his stomach. He thinks of the old man's pale wet eyes. In case it is explained later.

"And the boy before me," he says. "The Founder's. He was the key?"

"He was a key." Heng is watching him very carefully. "I do not think he was the only one. I think there was a second, a device, a thing the Founder made with his own hands, which the boy carried, and which was lost. The records are not clear. They speak of a cradle."

The word is in his mouth like a stone.

Jian does not move. He is perfectly aware that Qin Hao is looking at him now, in the doorway. He is aware of the brazier, and the lamp, and the silver pin humming in the lintel. He is aware of his own breath. He lets it go, very slowly, through his nose.

"I do not know what that is," he says.

"No." Heng's smile is thin. "I would be surprised if you did. It is simply a word in a scroll."

* * *

Qin Hao has risen.

He comes in from the doorway without a sound, and lays a hand on the back of Heng's chair. It is a light touch, almost fatherly. His tired eyes are on Jian, and there is something in them that was not there when he said I never found a conversation I could not learn from.

"I think that is enough for today," he says.

"Elder." Heng does not turn his head. "A moment. There is a second thing."

"You are tiring."

"I have been tired for ten months. A moment."

The Elder hesitates. Then he steps back.

Heng leans forward, a little, in the chair. His fingers have gone white on the arm. The gray scar at the angle of his jaw is moving, very faintly, as though something beneath it were turning over in its sleep, but his voice is steady.

"You called it a dock," he says.

Jian is silent.

"When you asked me about the fortieth step. You said: the dock. Not the lock. Not the plate. Not the door." The bright eyes do not leave his. "I have been reading the Founder's notes for eleven days, Lin Jian. I know every word he used for the mechanism of the stair. He called it a lock, a seal, a gate, a socket. He called it a door. He did not once use that word."

"I do not remember..."

"You said it as I have heard a man say spoon." The dry voice is almost wondering. "Without thought. As a thing that has a name. I have studied this Sect's founding for forty years. I have read the Founder's private notes, and the notes of his clerks, and the commentary of six hundred years of scholars. I have never seen the word dock. And I have never known a child to use it."

I did not say that. Jian's mind races back through the conversation, and finds it, a single syllable, dropped like a coin in the first minute, when he was wondering about the lock. I said it. In my head it was only a word.

It is a word from the other place.

He does not breathe.

"There is a thing in the notes," says Heng. "I did not understand it until now. A clerk wrote it in the margin, and did not dare to cross it out. The Founder's child spoke in strange words. He named things that had no names. The Founder said: he is not of this world." The thin hand lifts a little from the arm of the chair. "I thought it was a figure of speech."

"Elder."

Qin Hao's voice is very soft, and addressed to Jian.

"You do not have to answer," says the Elder. "It would be unjust to ask. Heng has been in the cold cells for eleven days, and he is a clever man who has built a great deal on a syllable." His long fingers close on the back of the chair. "Say nothing. I will see you out."

Jian looks at him. He looks at the dry kind tired face, and the beard, and the book. He thinks: he has heard it too.

He thinks: and he is going to let me leave.

"Thank you, Elder," he says.

"Do not thank me. I have not yet decided what I think." The old man's smile is rueful. "Go. Take your lamp."

He takes the lamp. He turns to the door. His legs, he finds, are perfectly steady, and he walks across the rug without hurry, through the silver-banded frame and out into the cold blue corridor. He is almost to the stair when the thin dry voice comes after him, from the room, clear and carrying.

"Lin Jian."

He stops.

"There is a third thing. I wished to give it to you for nothing, because you have given me something, though you do not know what." The voice has become very quiet. "Whatever it is that lives in your head. Whatever it is that speaks to you in words no one else can hear. I have read the Founder's last note." A pause. "It is older than the Sect."

The lamp does not shake in Jian's hand. The blue lights of the corridor do not flicker. But somewhere high above, in the cold dark of the Annex, a door closes, and the sound of it goes down through the stone like a bell.
